description: Somos un equipo dedicado en la realización de un juego interactivo que complemente la educacion y la experiencia interactiva, narrativa y creativa para futuros astronautas
summary:
Yaambesaj is a simulation of a lunar base, based on our challenge: to create an educational simulator for managing a lunar or Martian base. We focus on a lunar base. We aim to demonstrate management and assertive decision-making, which is important because every action has a reaction. This means managing resources (water, oxygen, energy, food, radiation protection, and communication and research time) in order to choose what is best for each situation.

It is an educational and interactive video game that brings space exploration closer to children between 7 and 12 years old, teaching them in a simple and fun way the challenges astronauts face to survive and work on the Moon.

The importance of the PLÉYADES lunar mission lies in letting children understand the real challenges of living outside Earth through an interactive experience. It shows that astronauts’ survival does not depend only on technology, but also on properly managing oxygen, water, energy and food.

It also makes complicated scientific topics easier to understand through a story, characters and situations that involve children in their learning, showing that decisions have consequences and that science helps us survive in space.
details:
Yaambesaj is an educational, interactive video game for children aged 7 to 12. It brings space exploration closer to them through an adventure in which every decision has consequences.

The story takes place in 2045. The player is an astronaut selected for a space mission called PLÉYADES. The goal is to travel to the Moon, expand a small scientific outpost and keep it running while facing the challenges of living away from Earth. PLÉYADES is a fictional mission inspired by NASA’s Artemis program, and the game says so.

The adventure begins with the launch from Earth and the journey to the Moon, guided by Mission Control. After landing, the astronaut meets Astro, a small fictional being who becomes the guide for the whole mission. Astro walks alongside the player, leads the way to each objective and shares scientific information in simple words. On the surface, the player explores the area and builds the systems needed to survive: solar arrays and batteries, water recycling, radiation shielding and a greenhouse with crops that NASA has really grown on the International Space Station.

Building the outpost is only the beginning. Over 21 simulated days, the player completes seven missions about managing resources, keeping equipment working and keeping the crew safe. Along the way there are nine expeditions with Astro to places such as a permanently shadowed crater, a sunlit ridge and a lava cave, and three unplanned events: dust in the airlock, a moonquake and a micrometeoroid strike.

Decisions are not independent: their consequences carry into the following days. For example, during the three days of shadow, heating uses far more energy. The player must decide whether to switch off the greenhouse or the scanner, or will have arrived prepared with charged batteries. On the day of the solar storm, a clock runs while the crew chooses where to take cover. Before confirming a task, the game shows what it will cost, and the daily report explains what happened as cause and effect.

Some tasks are done by hand: pointing a solar panel at the Sun, brushing lunar dust away, drilling for a sample, watering and harvesting the crops. A lunar rover lets the player bring back ice and cargo from far away. Asking Mission Control for advice takes 2.6 seconds, because a radio message needs 1.3 seconds to reach Earth and 1.3 to return.

At the end of each mission, the game shows a score from 0 to 100% and how the decisions affected the outpost. If the essential systems fail, the mission is cancelled. The game then explains what went wrong, why, and what to try differently, and the player can restart. An easy mode gives younger players more margin.

To support learning, Yaambesaj includes a library of 55 fact cards, each with a link to its official source: 54 draw on 43 different NASA pages, and one on the Canadian Space Agency. Every number in the game is labelled as NASA data or as a game parameter. The solar storm is modelled on a real event from NASA’s DONKI database and is shown with its date as a historical event. The game also states that a solar alert is not the same as a radiation dose, and that the dose it uses is a simplified model. The submission form allows 25 NASA links; the full list of 43 NASA sources, with a link for each fact, is in the game’s NASA Data Library.

We want children to take part in space exploration instead of only reading about it. By facing these challenges they practise critical thinking, problem solving, planning and decision-making. They also learn why resources must be used responsibly, and how science and technology help people live away from Earth.

To develop Yaambesaj we used TypeScript 5.9 as the main language, HTML5 and CSS3 for the interface, and PlayCanvas 2.24 as the 3D engine, based on WebGL 2. We used Vite for development and building, Vitest for 48 automated tests, Node.js and npm as the development environment, and Git for version control. The project was developed on a Windows 11 computer.

The project was developed with artificial-intelligence assistance (Claude, by Anthropic, through Claude Code). The AI wrote the code, the texts and the code that generates the graphics and the sound, under the direction and review of the team. This is stated in the game’s Credits, and every illustration carries a visible mark.

All graphics, textures and sounds are generated by code in the browser; the game contains no image or audio files. The narrator uses the browser’s own synthetic voice. Progress is saved on the player’s device. The scientific information comes from official NASA sources, including solar-activity records from DONKI, and from the Canadian Space Agency for food production. The game is published online and works in modern browsers on computers and mobile devices, with no installation or account.

What sets Yaambesaj apart is the combination of an adventure story with a simulation of scientific decisions. The player does not just receive information. The player explores a 3D environment, interacts with Astro and takes part in building and running a lunar outpost. A decision can solve one problem and affect other resources at the same time. This allows learning through experience, seeing the consequences and trying again.

The project’s creativity also shows in how scientific information is woven into the story, with official data kept separate from the simplified values used in the game. The characters, settings and visual elements are generated through programming, combining artistic design with technical development.

During development we considered scientific accuracy, accessibility, privacy and the needs of young players. The interface shows three simple indicators by default (power, life and protection) in green, yellow or red, with the detailed numbers one tap away. The game offers subtitles, Spanish and English, large text, high contrast, reduced motion, controls for computer and touch screens, and several graphics quality levels.

We also kept a clear line between fiction and science. Astro is a fictional character, and the game states it; the space information is presented with references to official sources. The game does not collect personal data and uses no accounts, tracking or advertising. Automated tests check the missions, the simulation, both languages and the scientific references.

With this project we hope to spark children’s curiosity about science, technology and space exploration, and to show that learning about them can be fun. We hope they finish the experience understanding that a space mission is not only about travelling to another world. It is also about making responsible decisions to keep people safe and make good use of what is available.

We also want what they learn to connect with everyday life: caring for water, using energy responsibly and planning before acting. In the long term, Yaambesaj aims to encourage new generations’ interest in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM), motivating them to explore, ask questions and look for solutions to the challenges of the future.
